steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper presenting MicroRes, a framework that profiles the resilience of microservice systems by measuring how degradation spreads from system metrics to user-aware metrics. Explain why current rule-based resilience profiling falls short, our key observation, the framework, the evaluation results, and the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Microservice systems and their attributes
- Resilience and why profiling it matters
- Current practice: manual resilience rules and its two problems
- Challenge and key insight: degradation dissemination
- MicroRes overview
- Evaluation results
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Microservice systems
  - online service = many fine-grained, independently-managed microservices
  - three attributes: highly decoupled, many microservices (Netflix: hundreds to thousands); dynamic (continuous, frequent features/updates); specialized (one request type each)
  - microservices interact to serve users' requests
- Resilience
  - definition: maintain acceptable performance and recover service under failures
  - Figure 1: throughput of an online service in normal vs faulty period; failure -> throughput decrement -> low resilience
  - faults/failures unavoidable; resilient system can be commissioned by ensuring reliability
  - without sufficient resilience, new/updated system shouldn't go to production
- Current practice: manual resilience rules
  - rules: failure types, metrics to monitor, degradation measure, pass/fail criteria
  - time-consuming, labor-intensive, inflexible
  - problem 1, domain expertise: huge number of microservices (up to tens of thousands) and failures; dynamism -> frequent rule updates; Huawei Cloud: two man-months of discussion to agree on rules (our survey)
  - problem 2, no fit across systems: specialized microservices -> manifold failures/manifestations; fixed PASS/FAIL can't capture subtle differences; resilience mechanisms (circuit breakers, replications, node auto-scaling) on platforms like Kubernetes -> "gray-failure" status not captured by metrics like MTTR
- Challenge and insight
  - goal: versatile resilience profiling with smooth criteria; non-trivial
  - challenge: to what extent is a system resilient?
  - study: Train-Ticket benchmark, two deployments with/without resilience mechanisms (Section § 3.2)
  - failures affect system performance metrics (memory usage, network throughput); resilient service stops impact spreading to user-aware metrics (response latency, MTTR)
  - insight: measure resilience by degree of degradation dissemination; no dissemination = high resilience
- MicroRes
  - first versatile resilience profiling framework for microservices
  - three phases: failure execution; dissemination-based metric lattice search; resilience indexing
  - failure execution: injection + clearance; with given failure and load generator, collect metrics in normal and faulty period
  - lattice search: rank metrics by contribution to overall degradation; lattice from power set of metric set; degradation-based path search
  - indexing: resilience in (0,1) by how much system-metric degradation reaches user-aware metrics
- Evaluation
  - Train-Ticket and Social-Network (open source), Huawei Cloud (industrial)
  - inject failures, compare with baselines; accurate, outperforms baselines
  - cross-entropy: 0.3246 Train-Ticket, 0.3766 Social-Network, 0.2977 industrial
  - accuracy: 0.9012, 0.8611, 0.8929
  - used in Huawei Cloud production; code and dataset public
- Contributions
  - identify labor-intensity and flexibility issues; first investigation of degradation dissemination in resilient vs non-resilient systems
  - MicroRes: automatically indexes resilience to different failures; higher dissemination = lower resilience
  - evaluation on two open-source + one industrial system; industrial case study

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Nowadays an online service is usually developed as a bunch of fine-grained microservices that are managed independently, and then deployed as a microservice system. Microservice systems have three prominent attributes. First, they are highly decoupled and usually have many microservices, e.g., the system of Netflix has hundreds to thousands of microservices. Second, microservices are dynamic, new features and updates are delivered continuously and frequently. Last, microservices are specialized, so each microservice processes only one type of request. The microservices interact with each other and together they serve the requests of users.

Resilience is the ability to keep performance at an acceptable level and to recover the service back to normal under service failures, and it is one of the abilities that online services essentially need. Figure 1 shows an example that is not resilient, by plotting the request throughput of an online service during the normal period and the faulty period. Intuitively the resilience of this service is low, because the failure causes service degradation, which we can see as a decrement in throughput. So resilience profiling is crucial, because faults and failures cannot be avoided, and a resilient system can be commissioned to users by ensuring service reliability. If the resilience is not high enough, a new or updated microservice system should not be deployed directly in the production environment.

The current practice for resilience profiling is to set resilience rules by hand, including which failure types are concerned, the metrics to monitor, how degradation is measured, and the criteria for passing or failing the tests. But this method takes a lot of time and labor, and it also lacks the flexibility to adapt to different microservice systems.

First, identifying rules manually relies a lot on domain expertise to define rules that can represent the degradation that failures cause. Defining good rules is a big burden because 1) there are usually a huge number of microservices (up to tens of thousands), and so also of failures, because microservices are highly decoupled; 2) because microservices are dynamic, the rules have to be updated frequently. According to our survey, in Huawei Cloud it usually takes two man-months of discussion for the test engineers to reach a consensus on the rules, and the need for updates makes this even worse.

- insight: study two deployments of Train-Ticket (open-source benchmark), with/without common resilience mechanisms (Section § 3.2); failures affect system performance metrics (memory usage, network throughput) but resilient service stops the impact reaching user-aware metrics (response latency, MTTR); measure resilience by degree of degradation dissemination: no dissemination = high resilience, otherwise low
- MicroRes: first versatile resilience profiling framework; phases: failure execution (injection + clearance, collect metrics in normal and faulty period with given failure and load generator), dissemination-based metric lattice search (rank metrics by contribution to degradation; lattice from power set of metrics; degradation-based path search), resilience indexing in (0,1)
- evaluation: Train-Ticket, Social-Network, Huawei Cloud; beats baselines; cross-entropy 0.3246 / 0.3766 / 0.2977; accuracy 0.9012 / 0.8611 / 0.8929; used in Huawei Cloud production; code and data public
- contributions:
  - identify labor-intensity and flexibility issues; first investigation of degradation dissemination in resilient vs non-resilient systems
  - MicroRes indexes resilience automatically; higher dissemination = lower resilience
  - evaluation on two open-source + one industrial system; industrial case study

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Nowadays an online service is usually developed as a bunch of fine-grained microservices that are managed independently, and then deployed as a microservice system. Microservice systems have three prominent attributes. First, they are highly decoupled and usually have many microservices, e.g., the system of Netflix has hundreds to thousands of microservices. Second, microservices are dynamic, new features and updates are delivered continuously and frequently. Last, microservices are specialized, so each microservice processes only one type of request. The microservices interact with each other and together they serve the requests of users.

Resilience is the ability to keep performance at an acceptable level and to recover the service back to normal under service failures, and it is one of the abilities that online services essentially need. Figure 1 shows an example that is not resilient, by plotting the request throughput of an online service during the normal period and the faulty period. Intuitively the resilience of this service is low, because the failure causes service degradation, which we can see as a decrement in throughput. So resilience profiling is crucial, because faults and failures cannot be avoided, and a resilient system can be commissioned to users by ensuring service reliability. If the resilience is not high enough, a new or updated microservice system should not be deployed directly in the production environment.

The current practice for resilience profiling is to set resilience rules by hand, including which failure types are concerned, the metrics to monitor, how degradation is measured, and the criteria for passing or failing the tests. But this method takes a lot of time and labor, and it also lacks the flexibility to adapt to different microservice systems.

First, identifying rules manually relies a lot on domain expertise to define rules that can represent the degradation that failures cause. Defining good rules is a big burden because 1) there are usually a huge number of microservices (up to tens of thousands), and so also of failures, because microservices are highly decoupled; 2) because microservices are dynamic, the rules have to be updated frequently. According to our survey, in Huawei Cloud it usually takes two man-months of discussion for the test engineers to reach a consensus on the rules, and the need for updates makes this even worse.

Second, rule-based resilience profiling cannot fit different microservice systems. There are two reasons for this: 1) Microservices are specialized for different business applications, which makes the failures and how they manifest manifold. 2) The fixed PASS/FAIL results from resilience test rules cannot tell apart subtle differences in the resilience of an online service when the boundary between "resilient" and "non-resilient" is less absolute. This happens because many refined resilience mechanisms (e.g., circuit breakers, replications, and node auto-scaling) are applied in existing platforms like Kubernetes, so the system can be in a "gray-failure" status that a few common metrics used in the test rules, like mean time to recover (MTTR), cannot fully depict.

An intuitive idea to mitigate these two issues is a versatile resilience profiling technique with smooth criteria. But designing such an approach is not trivial. The critical challenge is how to determine how resilient a microservice system is. To address this challenge we investigate the impact of failures on two deployments of Train-Ticket, an open-source microservice benchmark system, one with and one without common resilience mechanisms (Section § 3.2). We find that failures affect system performance metrics such as memory usage and network throughput, but a resilient service can stop the impact from disseminating to user-aware metrics such as response latency and MTTR. Based on this observation, our insight is that we can measure microservice resilience by comparing how much degradation disseminates from system performance metrics to user-aware metrics. If the degradation cannot disseminate from system performance metrics to user-aware metrics, the resilience is high. If it can, the resilience is low.

Motivated by this insight we present MicroRes, which is the first versatile resilience profiling framework for microservice systems. MicroRes has three phases: failure execution, dissemination-based metric lattice search, and resilience indexing. Failure execution has two phases, failure injection and failure clearance. Given a specified failure and a predefined load generator, MicroRes collects the monitoring metrics of the service in the normal period and in the faulty period. For the dissemination-based metric lattice search, we propose a dissemination-based algorithm that ranks all the monitoring metrics by their contributions to the overall degradation of the service. We build a metric lattice from the power set of the set of monitoring metrics, and the ranking is based on a degradation-based path search in this metric lattice. Lastly, for resilience indexing, we index the resilience in (0,1) by how much of the degradation in system performance metrics is disseminated to the user-aware metrics.

Experiments on two open-source microservice systems (Train-Ticket and Social-Network) and one industrial one (Huawei Cloud) show that MicroRes is effective. We inject failures into all the systems and compare resilience profiling under MicroRes and several baselines. The results show that our method quantifies system resilience accurately and outperforms the baselines. In terms of cross-entropy, MicroRes gets the best performance of 0.3246 on the Train-Ticket benchmark, 0.3766 on the Social-Network benchmark, and 0.2977 on the industrial benchmark. In terms of accuracy MicroRes also gets the best performance, 0.9012, 0.8611, and 0.8929 on the Train-Ticket, Social-Network, and industrial benchmarks. We also show the successful usage of MicroRes in the production cloud system of Huawei Cloud. The code and dataset are publicly available.

The contributions of this work are the following:

- • We identify the labor-intensity and flexibility issues of the current rule-based practice for resilience profiling. Then we do the first investigation of how degradation disseminates from system performance metrics to user-aware metrics in resilient and non-resilient microservice systems, which shows that versatile resilience measuring is viable.

- • We propose MicroRes, the first versatile resilience profiling framework, which can automatically index the resilience of a microservice system to different failures. MicroRes measures how much degradation disseminates from system performance metrics to user-aware metrics. The higher the dissemination, the lower the resilience.

- • We evaluate MicroRes on two open-source microservice systems and one industrial one, and the results show it is effective and efficient. The industrial case study also confirms that MicroRes can be used in practice.

Second, microservices are dynamic: new features and updates are delivered continuously and frequently. Last, microservices are specialized, and each microservice only processes a single type of request. Microservices interact with each other to serve users' requests together.

Given a specified failure and a predefined load generator, MicroRes collects the service's monitoring metrics in the normal and faulty periods. For the dissemination-based metric lattice search, we propose a dissemination-based algorithm that ranks all monitoring metrics according to their contributions to the overall service degradation. We construct a metric lattice from the power set of the monitoring metric set, and the ranking is based on a degradation-based path search in the metric lattice. Lastly, for resilience indexing, we index the resilience in (0,1) by how much of the degradation in system performance metrics is disseminated to the user-aware metrics.

Experiments on two open-source (Train-Ticket [9] and Social-Network [10]) and one industrial (Huawei Cloud) microservice system demonstrate the effectiveness of MicroRes. We inject failures into all systems and compare the performance of resilience profiling under MicroRes and several baselines. The experimental results show that our method accurately quantifies system resilience and outperforms the baselines. Specifically, in terms of cross-entropy, MicroRes achieves the best performance of 0.3246 on the Train-Ticket benchmark, 0.3766 on the Social-Network benchmark, and 0.2977 on the industrial benchmark. In terms of accuracy, MicroRes also achieves the best performance of 0.9012, 0.8611, and 0.8929 on the Train-Ticket, Social-Network, and industrial benchmarks. Furthermore, we showcase the successful usage of MicroRes in the production cloud system of Huawei Cloud. We make the code and dataset publicly available.

The contributions of this work are highlighted as follows:

- • We identify the labor-intensity and flexibility issues of the current rule-based practice for resilience profiling. We then conduct the first investigation on how degradation disseminates from system performance metrics to user-aware metrics in resilient and non-resilient microservice systems, which demonstrates the viability of versatile resilience measuring.

- • We propose MicroRes, the first versatile resilience profiling framework that can automatically index the resilience of a microservice system to different failures. MicroRes measures the dissemination of degradation from system performance metrics to user-aware metrics. The higher the dissemination, the lower the resilience.

- • Evaluation of MicroRes on two open-source and one industrial microservice system indicates its effectiveness and efficiency. The industrial case study further confirms the practical usage of MicroRes.
